podcast.body: Featured on the album "Transformer," this significant song serves as a list of notable characters from Andy Warhol's Factory. It delves into their "bad influence" or "bad lives," referencing them by their specific names and alluding to their misfortunes or misbehavior. The song may also reflect Lou Reed's post-Velvet Underground resentment and "true hatred" towards Andy Warhol. "De hecho, tenemos esa gran canción que era Walk on the White Side, de Luric que viene a hablar es una lista de todos esos grandes personajes de la factoria y un poco de la mala influencia o de la mala vida que llevaban todos ellos."

podcast.body: This song, released in November 1972, became a genuine Top 40 hit and an AM radio success on both sides of the Atlantic, despite its "raunchy references." The lyrics recounted true stories of individuals in Andy Warhol's circle, including Holly Woodlawn (a transsexual from Miami), Candy Darling (another transsexual), and Joe Campbell, referred to as the "Sugar Plum Fairy." The first version of the song was recorded with drumsticks, but it was later re-recorded using brushes to achieve a "smoky, sleazy nightclub feel." The saxophone part at the end was played by Ronnie Ross, who had taught David Bowie saxophone in the 1950s. The iconic sliding bass line was created by session player Herbie Flowers, who layered two bass lines—one from a stand-up double bass and another from a fretless electric. Flowers was reportedly paid $30 for his contribution, and the bass line has since been sampled countless times in hip-hop and dance songs worldwide. "Released in November 1972 and an AM radio hits on both sides of the Atlantic, despite all the raunchy references that's Lou Reed and walk on the wild side."

podcast.body: This surprising Top 40 hit from 1972 became a landmark in popular culture for its open portrayal of sexuality and gender roles. The song name-checked real-life figures from Andy Warhol's circle, including drag queens Hollywood Lawn, Candy Darling, and Jackie Curtis, as well as gay actors Joe Delosandro (referred to as "Little Joe") and Joe Campbell (referred to as "Sugarplum Ferry"). "This song, surprisingly, shockingly, was a major top 40 hit."

podcast.body: This song technically made Lou Reed a one-hit wonder on the Hot 100. It was produced by David Bowie and was climbing the Hot 100 concurrently with Bowie's "Space Oddity," with the two songs at one point just two positions away from each other (Reed at #19, Bowie at #21). "The man who produced walk on the wild side was in the top 40 with his first major US hit. At the same time, walk on the wild side was in the top 40. That man was David Bowie."
